newsitem.title: CHINA: HK stocks set for slide amid currency jitters.
newsitem.headline: HK stocks set for slide amid currency jitters.

text.p: Hong Kong stocks look set to suffer a slide in prices on Tuesday as jitters about the stability of the Hong Kong dollar and Wall Street stocks rock sentiment and send investors looking for safer ground.

Concerns about a speculative attack on the Hong Kong dollar sent share prices into a tailspin on Friday. The Hong Kong dollar was stable at firmer levels on Tuesday but interest rates were rising in the one through three month forwards.
Ben Kwong, director of research at Dharmala Securities, said the Hang Seng Index could drop to 15,300 points in the short-term and was likely to test 15,500 points on Tuesday.
The Hang Seng Index slid 400.83 points on Friday to close at 16,096.88.

The market was closed on Monday for a holiday but Hong Kong stocks traded in London continued the decline with the Hang Seng London Reference Index shedding a total 761.93 points on Friday and Monday to close at 15,334.95.
"Hong Kong stocks, no doubt about it, will experience quite a sharp correction. Investors are still concerned about currency stability and also the stability of Wall Street," said Kwong.
The Dow Industrials suffered a setback on Friday, tumbling 247.37 points, or 3.11 percent.

The local market was unable to react on Monday and brokers said a rebound in Wall Street share prices overnight could limit Hong Kong's losses on Tuesday. The Dow Industrials gained 108.70 points, or 1.41 percent, overnight to close at 7,803.36.
"It would hve been a worse day had the U.S market not come back," said Kent Rossiter, institutional sales manager at Nikko Securities.

But he said the focus would be on the Hong Kong dollar, which was quoted at HK$7.74 against the U.S. dollar compared with HK$7.75 on Friday. Interest rates were at a high level with HongKong Bank quoting the overnight rate at 6.50/8.50 percent.

"If the Hong Kong dollar is not seen as being stable, then people will move out of the market and into other markets," said Rossiter. "Singapore has a chance of attracting some of the funds. It is typically seen as safer market," he said.
Brokers expected selling across the board with interest rate sensitive stocks leading the way.

"Investors are concerned that the currency crisis will trigger an upward interest rate trend. The big gainers in the past will be a target for profit-taking like banking and property stocks," said Kwong.
